problem: Evaluating language-guided robot policies on physical robots is costly because i.i.d. test instances require heavy scene resets, so experimenters usually run small, non-i.i.d. demonstrations that cover little of the instruction/scene space and give little insight into failure modes.
motivation: The space of language commands and scenes grows combinatorially, and real-world evaluation effort (moving furniture and objects) limits how many instances can be tested. Contrast sets from NLP suggest that small, targeted perturbations of i.i.d. test instances can probe local decision boundaries cheaply, which could give more trials per unit effort plus diagnostic insight.
key_idea: Apply cheap, minimal perturbations to language, scene and expected behavior of i.i.d. test instances (contrast sets) so that more trials can be run per unit of experimenter reset cost, while still estimating full-test-set performance and revealing policy sensitivities.
insight: Different perturbation types bias the estimate in different directions (language-behavior perturbations underestimate, scene-behavior perturbations overestimate SPL in Language-Table), so combining all types gives the closest estimate to the full test set. Per-perturbation performance differences expose specific brittleness, e.g. the Language-Table policy fails direction inversion (Delta LB2) and the real VLN-CE policy is fragile to rewording (Delta L). A limited-intervention baseline (no scene resets) is cheap but a poor estimator, showing that perturbing i.i.d. anchors matters.
method: Perturbation taxonomy: four functions, Delta L (language changes, behavior same), Delta LB (language changes, behavior differs), Delta S (scene changes, behavior same), Delta SB (scene changes, behavior differs).
Strategy Gamma(X) under a cost budget K: for each i.i.d. test instance, apply perturbations sequentially without resetting the scene, stopping when cumulative cost exceeds K (Algorithm 1).

Cost function: experimenter effort measured as distance (meters) objects are moved during scene changes; time to perturb the scene is also tested as an alternative cost. Language perturbations cost nothing.

Language-Table instantiation: 250 sampled instances over 5 task categories, 3 seeds; LB1 swaps source and target block references, LB2 flips direction words, SB1 moves the target block, SB2 moves the source block; metric is SPL against an optimal planner.

Real VLN-CE instantiation: five participants designed 5 furniture setups with narrated two-subgoal instructions; four perturbations (rephrase, change final goal, move a passive object, move the goal or block the path) give 20 new instances, and 75 runs in total with 3 repeats; metric is progress toward two subgoals (50% each).
Baselines: Standard i.i.d. evaluation and Limited Intervention (sequential new instructions without scene resets, unless the planner deems the instruction infeasible).

setting.backbone: Language-Table: pretrained FiLM-conditioned ResNet BC policy (LAVA not used); Real: VLN-CE policy pretrained in Habitat on RxR, fine-tuned on real-world data
setting.training_data: Language-Table: provided BC dataset; VLN-CE: RxR training set in Habitat plus a small set of real-world examples from one scene arrangement (behavior cloning, teacher forcing)
setting.observation: Language-Table: simulated top-down RGB with instruction; Real: egocentric RGB (and language) on a Locobot
setting.action_space: Language-Table: continuous end-effector pushing actions; VLN-CE: discrete FORWARD, TURN-LEFT 30°, TURN-RIGHT 30°, STOP
setting.simulator: Language-Table simulator; Habitat for VLN-CE pretraining; real-world testing on a Locobot
setting.privileged: Optimal planner used to compute SPL in Language-Table and to judge instruction feasibility for the limited-intervention baseline; otherwise none

numbers.method: Original instruction (5 i.i.d. instances x 3 runs)

numbers_note: The Language-Table SPL and cost-vs-error results are only shown in figures, with no numbers in the text beyond a standard-evaluation cost of 281 m for 250 trials. The Table 1 column labels (Delta V, Delta T) differ from the text's Delta S / Delta LB notation. Rows combining Delta L with Delta T (SR 30, 55.0) and Delta V with Delta T (SR 40, 65.0) are omitted from the numbers.
results: In Language-Table, combining all four perturbation types tracks the full-test-set SPL best and allows about 380 trials at the cost of 250 standard trials (281 m), and every perturbation strategy beats the Limited Intervention baseline as an estimator. On the real robot, one perturbation costs about 1 m per instance versus 8.8 m per standard instance, so 4x5=20 extra trials come for roughly 1 m each. Contrast-set evaluation gives roughly triple the trials at a 35 m budget and converges near the standard-evaluation estimate.
limitations: Assumes a representative i.i.d. test set exists and that perturbations stay inside the test domain; it does not estimate performance outside it.
Very small real-world scale (5 instances, 75 runs, one policy, one lab environment) and sim experiments use a single policy; only the sample mean is estimated, not the population mean.
Perturbations are hand-designed and task-specific, and limited to two tasks (Language-Table and VLN-CE); performance estimates depend on the perturbation mix, since some types bias them.
